uncited: This method generates initial camera rays for a frame by launching a compute shader with one thread per pixel.
It converts thread indices into normalized UV coordinates and computes ray directions using a pinhole camera model defined by a focal length.
*   Window width $W$ and height $H$ (integers).
*   Field of view angle $\alpha$ (radians).
*   Ray direction $\vec{rd}$ (world space, normalized).
*   No persistent data structures are required for ray generation itself.
*   Focal length $f$: Derived from $\alpha$.
Determine the pixel coordinates $(x, y)$ from the thread ID.
*   $x = \text{GroupID}_x \times 8 + \text{GroupThreadID}_x$
*   $y = \text{GroupID}_y \times 8 + \text{GroupThreadID}_y$
Scale the integer pixel coordinates to the range $[0, 1]$.
Shift the coordinates so the center of the screen is $(0,0)$.
The top-left pixel maps to $[-1, 1]$ and the bottom-right to $[1, -1]$.
Let $u = \vec{uv}_x$ and $v = \vec{uv}_y$.
Calculate the focal length $f$ based on the field of view $\alpha$.
Compute the initial unoriented ray direction $\vec{rd}^0$ in a local coordinate system where the camera looks along the positive Z-axis.
The ray origin is fixed at the camera center in the local coordinate system.
Transform $\vec{rd}^0$ and $\vec{o}_{origin}$ into world space using rotation matrices defined by camera angles $\phi$ and $\theta$.
Typically, this involves composing yaw and pitch rotations.
The implementer must define the rotation convention (e.g., intrinsic vs. extrinsic axes).
Floating point precision for $u, v$ depends on the window size.
For very large resolutions, $u^2 + v^2 + f^2$ may suffer from precision loss if $f$ is very small or very large.
*   **Boundary Pixels:** The mapping ensures all pixels from $(0,0)$ to $(W-1, H-1)$ are covered.
*   **Time Complexity:** $O(1)$ per pixel.
The computation involves a constant number of arithmetic operations (normalization, trigonometry, normalization).
*   **Memory Complexity:** $O(1)$ per thread.
No additional memory is allocated for ray generation.
Suitable for real-time applications where ray generation is a small fraction of the total rendering cost.
Does not account for lens effects (bokeh, distortion) without extension.
This method originates from implementations of GPU-based raycasting and raymarching, specifically those utilizing compute shaders for general-purpose rendering tasks.
The approach of mapping thread IDs to pixel coordinates and generating rays via a pinhole model is a standard technique in GPU ray tracing pipelines.
